title: Where To Drink in NYC Right Now (September 2026)
summary:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors. Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Bar Monto, Tin’s, Titán, Frenzie, Zig Zag Oyster Bar, and Mash Inn.

content:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors.

Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Bar Monto, Tin’s, Titán, Frenzie, Zig Zag Oyster Bar, and Mash Inn.

Bar Chimera

550 Madison Ave, New York, NY 10022

Part of Gracious Hospitality’s massive Midtown expansion — including a new location of Cote and a forthcoming omakase restaurant — Bar Chimera brings together three distinct drinking concepts: Martinis, whiskey, and wine. The luxurious space focuses on splurge-worthy drinks including an extensive program of aged Madeiras, special pours of hard-to-find wines and spirits, and classic Martinis made with meticulously thought-out ingredients, even down to the water used to dilute the drink.

Website

Stone & Soil

124 E 28th St, New York, NY 10016

Stone & Soil is a new cocktail bar that draws inspiration from Japanese flavors, design, and hospitality. Though it’s located within the Park South Hotel, you would never guess you’re in the middle of buzzy NoMad while sitting in the tranquil, minimalist space. The bar offers an extensive list of 22 complex cocktails that bend what you might expect from the classics, including the Bitter Sweet Mango, a White Negroni riff enhanced with mango and spice, and the Berry Pop Tart, a twist on the Hanky Panky that evokes tart red berries.

Website

Love Thy Neighbor

55 Christopher St, New York, NY 10014

Good news for fans of uptown institutions like Harlem’s (now closed) ROKC and Upper East Side haunt for ramen and flashy drinks NR: Owner and bartender Shigefumi Kabashima just opened a new cocktail concept in the West Village. Like his previous spots, the all-day bar and dining destination is rooted in Japanese craftsmanship and flavors, but also draws inspiration from the New York City community. Expect out-there concoctions like the Tokyo Banana, made with banana-infused whiskey, vermouth, milk brew coffee, shio koji, and miso powder; and the Wagyu Coke, the soda pop riff featuring wagyu-fat-washed bourbon, house cola syrup, and clarified black cherry purée.

Website

Somssi

79 MacDougal St, New York, NY 10012

Somssi is a new restaurant from the team at NA:EUN Hospitality — the group behind acclaimed concepts Atoboy, Atomix, and NARO — spearheaded by the group’s former director of operations Ahris Kim. Between the diverse menu of shareable plates and the extensive selection of wine, sake, and cocktails, there are countless pairing permutations to be made here. One that calls to us is the Potato, Potato, Potato, and caviar, which neatly wraps a creamy pomme purée with thin, crispy potato strings, topped with a heap of caviar, of course, which we’re sure would go well with a sparkling wine from the Finger Lakes or even a spritzy sake. The menu is a treasure trove of interesting beverages, so whichever combo you go with, it’s bound to be a delightful drinking experience.

Website

Dean’s

213 6th Ave, New York, NY 10014

Just when we thought NYC’s Guinness mania couldn’t go any longer, Dean’s arrives in the West Village ready to pour you a perfect — and sometimes even oyster-topped — pint. The British pub-inspired spot from Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi of King stays true to its theme with dishes like fish and chips, stargazy pie, and pork scratchings plus a list of English sparkling to wash it all down.

Website

Noury

137 Sullivan St, New York, NY 10012

From Lina Goujjane and Alex Chang, the wife-and-husband team behind Hudson Square’s Kiko, Noury combines elements of a modern Japanese izakaya with those of a wine and sake bar. Here, guests can pair small bites like the daily selection of sashimi or the house vegetable futomaki with rare bottles of sake or splurge-worthy Champagnes.

Website

Stars

139 E 12th St, New York, NY 10003

Stars is a new bar from the team behind beloved East Village wine destinations Claud and Penny. With their acclaimed food menus, the previous openings might have had diners asking the (seemingly eternal) question, “Is this a wine bar or a restaurant?” But Stars provides a clear example of a classic wine bar, with just 12 seats for guests to sit and enjoy a glass of Chasselas or Spätburgunder while snacking on deviled eggs. The list was also designed to make the wine bar experience more accessible, offering a rotating selection of 88 wines under $88 and by-the-glass options between $11 and $19. It’s walk-in only, but we recommend showing up early to put your name down for one of its highly coveted barstools.

Website

Banshee

143 1st Ave, New York, NY 10003

Longtime East Village bartender Jen Murphy opened Banshee with her neighborhood regulars in mind, focusing on just three things: Guinness, Martinis, and oysters. Sounds like a recipe for success to us. The Irish-influenced bar pours a stellar pint — Guinness is actually the only beer it has on draft — and offers a full menu of Martini options. Consider this your new go-to spot for a casual drink or lively nightcap in the EV.

Website

Bar Monto

61 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003

If you’ve been keeping up with New York’s boom in modern Irish pubs, here’s another one to add to your list. Bar Monto is the latest laid-back spot slinging creamy pints of Guinness in custom glassware. Beyond beer, the bar also offers a fun list of straightforward yet complex cocktails like the Basque Connection, made with Boatyard Irish gin, sherry, Valentia Island Irish vermouth, tonic, and muddled orange. The space draws inspiration from the pubs and social clubs found in Ireland in the 1980s and ’90s and aims to be a center for community, collaborating with local artists and musicians for events.

Website

Tin’s

109 Ludlow St, New York, NY 10002

Tin’s is a multi-concept space from Philip Dizard and Mercury Tin, bringing together their love for New York bars and Shanghainese comfort food in a three-story experience that includes both a casual dumpling counter and high-end cocktail bar. Creative concoctions span from unexpected delights like the Timmy’s Brain Blaster, a bright-green frozen Cognac cocktail topped with salted mascarpone foam, to riffs on classics like the Dako-Ri, a classic Daiquiri made with maojian tea and lemongrass.

Website

Oriana

174 Mott St, New York, NY 10012

Oriana is the wood-fired follow-up to West Village restaurant The Noortwyck, from executive chef Andy Quinn and acclaimed sommelier Cedric Nicaise. The new Nolita spot focuses on live-fire cooking, with a menu of dishes prepared over a wood-fired grill. To accompany plates like the BBQ Duck Crown and Axe Handle Pork Chop, Oriana features a deep, 7,000-bottle cellar, primarily composed of classic European wines. Though there are certainly many opportunities to splurge, the program also features over 150 bottles under $100.

Website

Bar Chucho

37 Market St, New York, NY 10002

Fans of Corima’s Uni Gin Sour, rejoice! The (somewhat controversial) savory cocktail is making its return at Bar Chucho, a new bar from the team behind the acclaimed Mexican tasting menu spot that first dared to shake sea urchin with booze. Though the walk-in-only space has a more casual, cantina-like vibe, the high-concept cocktails and bar snacks still show off complex flavors. The drink menu includes riffs on classics like the Margarita with Granny Smith apple, Midori, and cilantro and a mezcal-based Sazerac with plantain and hoja santa. And we can’t forget the Uni Gin Sour — now served on draft — revamped with strawberry and yuzu. Bar snacks include a cheesy mushroom gringa, tuna chilindrina, and a dry-aged burger with bone marrow and burnt onion mayo.

Website

Gigi’s

138 Franklin St, Brooklyn, NY 11222

The (very French) team behind recently-shuttered chef haunt Fulgurances Laundromat just launched a new concept down the street. Gigi’s calls itself a “rôtisserie wine bar,” which is exactly what it sounds like. It has an extensive wine program and rôtisserie chickens available by the whole or the half, each served on a silver platter with roasted potatoes and a trio of dipping sauces. If you aren’t in the mood for a full meal, try the cheese plate with bread and poppy seed butter or the colorful dish of market pickles. The rotating by-the-glass options (including special magnum pours) are written on the mirrors on the wall and the bottle menu features a lengthy selection of options under $100, as well as many splurge-worthy picks.

Website

Arthur

132 Franklin St, Brooklyn, NY 11222

Another new addition to Greenpoint, Arthur inhabits the old Fulgurances Laundromat space (and is still donning the restored facade). Inspired by modern Parisian bistros, the neighborhood spot has a lively, welcoming atmosphere. Start with the freshly baked brioche and house-cultured butter alongside the Brioche Martini designed to mirror the dish with butter-washed gin, whey eau de vie, and toasty barley tea. Then move onto the wine list, which beverage director Charlotte Mirzoeff curated to feature small, thoughtful producers. We couldn’t help but notice the favorable pricing on the Champagnes here, so take that as a good excuse to dig into some grower bubbles.

Website

Peek Inn

38 Driggs Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11222

Peek Inn is a casual neighborhood bar in Greenpoint from the teams behind Williamsburg’s beloved burger joint Cozy Royale and popular Brooklyn butcher shop The Meat Hook. Unsurprisingly, meat is on the menu. You can find it in the form of dressed-up hot dogs, ham sliders, and even colossal stuffed clams. Stop by for the impressive happy-hour deals including $10 ’tinis and $5 beer-and-shot combos.

Website

Balera

442 Graham Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11211

Balera is a new destination in Williamsburg for reveling under a disco ball and swaying to a DJ, but not with a Vodka Soda in hand as you would at a typical late-night haunt. Instead, guests can enjoy Roman-style pizzas, Italian wines, and Parmigiano-washed Martinis while taking in the experience. Opened by five friends, the restaurant is inspired by the lively bars and eateries of their Italian beachside hometowns.

Website

Echo Lake

357 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211

This new two-story bar concept in Williamsburg is entirely focused on celebrating rum. The first floor, Echo Lake, showcases the versatile spirit in a range of cocktails, from classic spirit-forward creations to fruit-filled tropical drinks. It also offers a full menu of Daiquiri variations, including a rotating “Daily Daiquiri” for just $12. Head downstairs to Undercurrent to dive deeper into the spirit with special pours from rare and hard to find bottles.

Website

Kinda Nice

168 Borinquen Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11211

Known for their work behind the bar at Brooklyn’s beloved Grand Army, Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone are going out on their own with their new venture Kinda Nice. The welcoming Williamsburg cocktail bar brings the convivial feeling of an old-school neighborhood diner, with the food and drinks to match. The cocktails are based on classic diner favorites, including a Greek Salad ‘Tini and a Short Stack Margarita (with a choice between strawberry and blueberry flavors).

Website

Bodega Nights

425 Troutman St, Brooklyn, NY 11237

The team behind tiny Lower East Side wine bar Babysips just opened a new spot in Bushwick that ups the ante with a much larger space and food menu. Bodega Nights has an expansive front patio lined with rows of picnic tables for the warmer months — but if it’s too cold to sit outside, you can still embrace some natural light through the front wall’s top-to-bottom windows. It’s the kind of place you can stop by for a quick vermouth and soda, cocktail, or glass of Cava at the bar, or spend an evening exploring the concise, Euro-centric wine list. Chenin fans take note, when we went, six of the 12 white wines on offer by the bottle were Loire Valley Chenin Blancs.

Website

Titán

5 Front St, Brooklyn, NY 11201

With chef Alan Delgado of flour-tortilla destination Los Burritos Juarez designing the menu and esteemed bartender Ivy Mix, previously of beloved agave bar Leyenda and current co-owner of Whoopsie Daisy, shaking up drinks, Dumbo’s new Titán brings two buzzy names from New York’s food and drink scenes into one beautifully curated space. The drinks menu offers expertly executed classics like a Margarita and Michelada, as well as culinary-inspired cocktails like the Dirty Root, with bacanora and escabeche, and the frozen Charmagoy, which brings together tequila, tamarind, mango, and chamoy.

Website

Frenzie

129 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11201

 

The team behind Brooklyn’s Confidant is expanding with a casual pizza spot that caters to the late-night crowd. While Frenzie is sure to be a great place to enjoy a bottle of chilled red wine and a spicy vodka pie at any time, it’s worth noting that at 10 p.m. the restaurant offers a few combo deals that make for the perfect nightcap (every night out should end with a slice). The offer, available Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, pairs a cheese or pepperoni pie with either a pitcher of Narragansett beer, two Daiquiris, or two Martinis.

Website

Bar Heretic

270 Clermont Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11205

This new arrival to the Fort Greene neighborhood has two main focuses: freshly baked bread and natural wine. We suggest embracing both with a thick, airy hunk of focaccia or a slice of sourdough and a pour of whatever’s open. It’s open for walk-ins only from Thursdays through Sundays, making it a great spot to pop in for a glass.

Website

Grimm Tavern

659 Vanderbilt Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11238

Lauren and Joe Gimm, the couple behind East Williamsburg’s beloved brewery Grimm Artisanal Ales, recently debuted their new restaurant Grimm Tavern. Here guests can explore Grimm’s extensive list of beers alongside classic American tavern dishes like a dry-aged smash burger and a muffuletta. But it isn’t just for beer fans; the menu also features a selection of wines from Grimm’s project Physica Wines as well as a list of signature cocktails.

Website

Zig Zag Oyster Bar

406 Prospect Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11238

The team behind Lower East Side seafood hot spot Cervo’s now has a dedicated raw bar in Brooklyn. If indulging in a seafood tower could ever be considered casual, this vibey, walk-in only spot might be the place. Grab a seat on the sidewalk or along the space’s stunning curved bar and order an Original Martini or Bloody Mary to accompany the icy plates of oysters and shrimp cocktail.

Website

Bar Ferdinando

151 Union St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

Bar Ferdinando is an Italian bar and café that recently took over the space of beloved Carroll Gardens institution Ferdinando’s Focacceria, which served the neighborhood for 121 years. The revamped space pairs Sicilian snacks with classic aperitivo drinks and a wide selection of amari. It’s the ideal location for an afternoon of sipping Negronis, vermouth on the rocks, or even a strawberry-and-basil-infused Campari and Soda. And the refreshing drinks are the perfect pair for dishes like the pane e panelle, a sandwich stacked with crispy chickpea fritters, ricotta, and caciocavallo cheese, or the heaping plate of fries topped with garlicky clams.

Website

Tavern Next Door

327 Van Brunt St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

If you’ve ever found yourself waiting for over two hours to snag a bite of Red Hook Tavern’s thick, pepper-crusted burger, we have the cocktail bar for you. The meat-slinging team recently expanded with a next-door cocktail bar that not only features one of the city’s most coveted burgers, but a whimsical cocktail menu with brightly colored creations like the tall, neon Blue Hawaiian and a refined take on an Appletini.

Website

Mash Inn

1215 8th Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11215

Located in a former laundromat in Park Slope, Mash Inn is a new bar and beer counter from the team behind Gold Star in Prospect Heights. The casual spot offers a rotating menu of beers on draft that you can enjoy in the cozy record-filled space or order growlers to-go from the beer window. The bar also offers light snacks like cheese, pickles, and charcuterie to enjoy alongside the freshly poured pints.

Website

title: We Asked 9 Wine Pros: What’s the Most Underrated American Wine Region? (2026)
summary:
Scanning the shelves at a standard wine shop might make you think California is the only state making wine worth sipping. And while it’s true that Napa Valley and Sonoma County have some of the most famous wineries stateside, the U.S. is home to a wide swath of regions making excellent wine. Every single state in the U.S. produces wine, which means there are dozens of overlooked regions worth exploring, whether that means taking a trip to the vineyard or simply picking up a new bottle to try.

content:
Scanning the shelves at a standard wine shop might make you think California is the only state making wine worth sipping. And while it’s true that Napa Valley and Sonoma County have some of the most famous wineries stateside, the U.S. is home to a wide swath of regions making excellent wine.

Every single state in the U.S. produces wine, which means there are dozens of overlooked regions worth exploring, whether that means taking a trip to the vineyard or simply picking up a new bottle to try. So we asked sommeliers from across the country to name the region they’re most excited about right now that deserves a little more love. From underappreciated regions in upstate New York to pockets of the Pacific Northwest that remain off the beaten path, here are the most underrated American wine regions, according to sommeliers.

The most underrated American wine regions, according to sommeliers:

  • Hudson Valley, N.Y.
  • Northern Michigan
  • Ballard Canyon, Santa Barbara, Calif.
  • Laurelwood District, Willamette Valley, Ore.
  • San Luis Obispo Coast, Calif.
  • Yakima Valley and Walla Walla Valley, Wash.
  • Seneca Lake, N.Y.
  • Applegate Valley, Ore.

“The Hudson Valley is one of those wine regions that rewards curiosity because it has never had the luxury of taking an obvious path. The climate is challenging, the growing season is shorter, and the wines tend to have a freshness and restraint that I really love. They’re energetic, food-friendly, and often much more nuanced than people expect from the region. What makes the Hudson Valley particularly interesting to me is that it doesn’t feel like a smaller version of somewhere else: unlike Long Island’s maritime, Bordeaux-leaning wines or the Finger Lakes’ extraordinary Rieslings, the Hudson Valley has developed a more eclectic identity, with winemakers embracing everything from Cabernet Franc and Chardonnay to French-American hybrids. There’s a sense of experimentation and discovery there that feels distinctly American, and I think we’re only beginning to understand how compelling these wines can be.” —Vanessa Price, wine director, Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, N.Y.

“The most surprising (and certainly underrated) wines that I’ve tasted in the last few years have actually been from Northern Michigan. Patience, thoughtfulness, and collaborative approaches on the peninsula are really driving a renaissance for the wines here. Names like Dave Bos and Brian Ulbrich (Left Foot Charley) bring a real unbending commitment to growth in the industry, and produce wines that are tasty and, in many cases, improve with each consecutive vintage. Although Riesling is king here, I have tasted multiple compelling examples of other Alsatian varieties that thrive in this climate as well as some interesting and quaffable reds from grapes like Pinot Noir, Gamay, and Blaufränkisch. Paired with a blossoming restaurant and cocktail scene, Northern Michigan is a place to watch (and visit!).” —Erin Healy, head sommelier, Restaurant Daniel, New York City

“Ballard Canyon AVA is a small valley within Santa Barbara County whose wines still fly under the radar. The sandy limestone soils and wide diurnal range give the Syrah produced in Ballard Canyon both ripeness and a savory, peppery, Northern Rhône character. Producers like Stolpman, Beckmen, and Likha are making structured, characterful, age-worthy wines rather than the cliché California fruit bombs produced in other regions. It’s genuinely site-expressive, Rhône-style wine priced at true value for quality. The region is represented on our lists in all three cities.” —Dean Fuerth, beverage director, Sushi Nakazawa, Los Angeles, NYC, and Washington, D.C.

“As one of the newest AVAs in Willamette Valley, the Laurelwood District can easily fly under the radar. Laurelwood is the first AVA to be named after its unique soil type, and also hosts the highest elevation in the Willamette Valley. I find this AVA champions some of the best blue-fruit forward Pinot Noirs, like one of my go-to favorite producers, Ponzi Vineyards.” —Kyle Amoroso, head sommelier, Aqua Roma and Aqua Kyoto, NYC

“I am personally loving the wines coming out of the San Luis Obispo Coast AVA right now. The SLO Coast has only been recognized as an AVA for four-ish years, and it absolutely makes sense to have that designation. The microclimate there is super interesting to wine nerds with lots of fog, tons of sunshine, sea breezes, and calcareous soil. And with a very long growing season, the grapes have plenty of hang time on the vine to develop complexity of flavor and so much depth. The area focuses on Pinot Noir and Chardonnay (I’ve had Pinot Noir from here that rivaled Savigny-lès-Beaune elegance), but it is also home to a growing hotbed for Albariño. The coastal influence is essential to build beautiful and typical Albariños, and as this is one of my favorite grapes to drink, I am excited to see more becoming available domestically.” —Shannon LaDawn, sommelier, Husk, Savannah, Ga.

“Washington produces some of the Pacific Northwest’s most distinctive wines, from savory, expressive Syrah to vibrant, black-fruit-driven Cabernet Sauvignon. A dynamic wine country with a beautiful landscape, the region is shaped by the Cascade Mountains, home to Mount Rainier, which create a rain-shadow effect; the historic Missoula Floods, which gifted the region with distinctive soils; and the gorgeous Columbia River, which provides irrigation to most of the vineyards. My suggestion for AVAs to explore in this state would be Yakima Valley and Walla Walla Valley.” —Slim Melo, assistant wine director, Aman, NYC

“Ballard Canyon has become one of the California regions I’m most excited about. Stolpman Vineyards captures what makes the area special, especially with La Cuadrilla — a vibrant, approachable Syrah that showcases both the character of Ballard Canyon and the people behind the wine.” —Chuck Tatum, sommelier, Olivine, Auburn, Ala.

“When asked about the most underrated wine region in America, I always point to Seneca Lake. It continues to astonish me and others in the wine world with the quality of its site-specific Riesling production. Producers like the young, brilliant winemakers at Forge Cellars have demonstrated the potential for cru-like distinctions within Seneca Lake. The not-so-subtle differences in wines from individual lieux-dits express themselves beautifully and uniquely. The racy acidity of the Rieslings produced from sites like Leidenfrost nods to Germany, while offering a distinct complexity shaped by the region’s shale soils and unique mesoclimate. I’m always excited to taste wines from this region because of their singular character and the talented winemakers drawn to this remarkable landscape.” —Brittney Johnson, sommelier, Marbled & Fin, Savannah, Ga.

“I gave this a lot of thought, and I kept coming back to the Applegate Valley in Southern Oregon as one of the most underrated wine regions in the country. It has this great combination of warm days and cool nights that really seems to suit Rhône varieties, which I love. The wines can be generous and expressive, but still have tons of freshness and savory character. Troon Vineyard is a favorite of mine, especially their Mourvèdre. I first tasted it during my time at Gramercy Tavern, and it was one of those wines that really stuck with me. It was earthy and spicy, with so much fruit, but everything was so well integrated. I think I told the rep who I was tasting with that it’s a wine that makes you want to turn into a cartoon and cannon ball right in the glass. It was super compelling, and I kept going back for another sniff, and another sip. It completely opened my eyes to what Southern Oregon could do, and I think Troon captures a lot of what makes Applegate so exciting right now.” —Dorian González Vega, beverage director, Union Square Cafe, NYC

Is this a harmless and fun way to reward wine lovers and devotees, or is it yet another way to promote snobbery and elitism within wine?

title: The Psychology Behind Food Towers: Why Are We Drawn to Tiered Meals?
summary:
I am not a particularly holiday obsessed person. It is always my mushy husband who reminds me that it’s time to adorn our fake plastic tree and dust off the Menorah. Yet, if a seasonal invite involves both food and drama, then I will don a festive spirit and roll up. This philosophy is what landed me at a marble table in mid December last year, waiting for high tea service at Salt Lake City’s Grand America Hotel.

content:
I am not a particularly holiday obsessed person. It is always my mushy husband who reminds me that it’s time to adorn our fake plastic tree and dust off the Menorah. Yet, if a seasonal invite involves both food and drama, then I will don a festive spirit and roll up. This philosophy is what landed me at a marble table in mid December last year, waiting for high tea service at Salt Lake City’s Grand America Hotel.

A server with the verve of a freshly shaken can of Sprite delivered the classic three-tiered structure: berry-laced scones and snappy cookies on the bottom, puddings and miniature cheesecakes in the middle, and an array of unidentifiable sandos on the top. He stepped back from the table and looked at my two friends and I knowingly. Then this walking wink asked us coyly, “Who wants a photo with their tower?”

The truth is that the food was completely unremarkable. But surrounding us in the almost comically elegant dining room — with enough crystal chandeliers, polished silver, and cream-and-gold upholstery to make you feel like you’d accidentally wandered into a Downton Abbey set — fellow customers were behaving identically. Whipping out their phones, squintily aiming them at the tower of dainty bites, and locking in a fleeting moment of opulence.

This specialness is exactly what afternoon tea, ritualized in the 1840s by Anna, Duchess of Bedford, was meant to confer. But the three-tiered stand wasn’t a new invention so much as an evolution. As early as the 1720s, wealthy English households displayed fruit and sweetmeats on ornate silver epergnes that doubled as centerpieces. By the early 19th century, Marie-Antoine Carême was building elaborate architectural pièces montées from sugar, marzipan, and pastry. And later that century, Parisian brasseries popularized plateaux de fruits de mer, ancestors of modern seafood towers.

Today, the bacchanalia of vertical presentation has spilled into nearly every corner of modern dining. Across the country, restaurants are nestling pink shrimp, glistening oysters, and honking crab legs into icy layers; balancing waffles and eggs on tiered A-frames; and fashioning donuts into tabletop monuments. Bars are sending out trees laden with Espresso Martinis and blush glasses of rosé. Champagne towers are the nouveau wedding flex. And home cooking enthusiasts are coaxing piles of chips and hunks of salami into improbable, honey-drizzled pyramids.

No matter what it carries, we simply cannot seem to deflect the tower’s spell. So I brought one question to the restaurant designers, chefs, psychologists, neuroscientists, food stylists, and sculptors I interviewed for this story: Why? Their answers pointed to a united consensus. Food and drink towers have seduced us for centuries because they exploit several deeply human instincts at once. While the ingredients changed over time, the intent passed from generation to generation: elevate the food, elevate the occasion.

The Tallness Equation

The first clue in this psychological mystery has surprisingly little to do with food. Colin Ellard, a cognitive neuroscientist and professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo, studies the relationship between humans and built environments. Tallness, he says, has long been a shorthand for importance. “We assume this kind of equation between height, power, success, all the potent things of life,” Ellard tells me, explaining why skyscrapers inspire both awe and a sense of oppression. The association runs so deep that it’s shaped our language. “We make references to elevated experiences,” he says. “We don’t use that word by accident. It refers explicitly to height.”

Consumer research neatly validates the idea that we’re total simps to whatever looms over us. Studies on the marketing of luxury goods found that the higher a product sat on shelf, the more valuable and prestigious it appeared to the aspiring shoppers below.

“Through all the trauma that the world is experiencing, there’s such a need for whimsy.”

Towers may also inspire our reverence because, like a stalagmite rising upward from the floor of a cave, they seem to escape the ordinary condition of things. David Altmejd, a Montreal-born contemporary artist whose sculptures explore transformation and the human form, builds a piece skyward when he wants to transcend its materiality. “The natural state of matter is always as submissive to gravity; it naturally accumulates close to the ground, horizontally,” he tells me. “So the verticality of an object suggests that it’s something more than just material, as if it’s also spirit.”

We’ve always wanted to be seen looking cool. As towers entered the scene, dining rooms were becoming places to display wealth, taste, and social standing. Before the 1830s, hungry New Yorkers gathered in taverns, which doubled as third spaces to question “authority and governmental decisions,” historian Cindy R. Lobel writes in “Urban Appetites.” But as the city’s population boomed, its restaurant sector expanded and stratified. The new establishments, Lobel writes, “served as important spaces of social articulation — stages for acting out status and conspicuous consumption.” In other words, the tower is a natural extension of the very human desire to amass clout via luxury and extravaganza.

Attention Is the Point

Anyone with a propensity to doomscroll knows that we don’t remember everything we experience. Decades of research have shown that those we attend to — and process more deeply — are far more likely to persist in long-term memory. The difference between a meal that lodges itself in the mental filing cabinet upstairs and one that disappears the next day often comes down to how totally it commandeers attention.

Our lizard brains come with factory settings that respond to certain kinds of stimuli. We’re suckers for contrast, says Anna Polonsky, founder and creative director of restaurant design studio Polonsky & Friends, whether achieved “through scale, height, movement, light, color, or sound.” But the most powerful design principle — the one that draws accipiter-like stares from an entire restaurant — is interruption. “Anything that briefly disrupts the visual rhythm of a room invites notice,” she explains. A food tower rises above eye level, punctuates the landscape of a dining room, and, perhaps most importantly, “slows the moment down.”

That pause does a lot of work. Charles Spence, the Oxford experimental psychologist whose research on multisensory perception has informed the theatrical dining experiences at Heston Blumenthal’s Berkshire, England restaurant Fat Duck, argues that much of eating’s pleasure lies not in consumption but in anticipation. Well before the first bite, our brains are already predicting what a meal will taste like and how satisfying it will be. A food tower exploits that process from every angle.

It draws eyes while beelining through the dining room. Its relative height makes the contents seem fancy. And the quantity of food signals abundance without gluttony. As Spence puts it, “A tower offers a way to show a whole lot of food without the implication being that it’s all for one person.” Add movement — fizzy Champagne cascading into waiting glasses, for example — and a tower becomes even harder to ignore. “Dynamic food in motion is more attractive to your brain,” Spence says, citing the sizzling burgers and oozing sauces in fast-food advertisements.

A Touch of Whimsy

Some of today’s towers would likely make Duchess Anna roll in her grave. In Newport, R.I., where seafood stacks are practically part of the natural habitat, Brad Head decided to adapt the format to the hot dogs, burgers, and Espresso Martinis he shills at Wally’s Wieners. The result is deliberately absurdist: a tower of franks feels less like precious luxury and more like adult playtime. “It’s really about the experience that the guest has when they come,” Head says. “The food is kind of complementary to that.”

That sense of occasion is exactly what customers are chasing right now. In January this year, OpenTable reported a 46 percent year-over-year increase in experiential dining and an 11 percent rise in group bookings of six or more people. Over half of respondents said they would willingly pay more for a meal with a distinctive atmosphere. And even the physical space has become part of the performance: 58 percent of those surveyed now consider a restaurant’s “Instagram- or TikTok-worthiness” when deciding where to eat.

Perhaps food towers also satisfy a deeper human yearning. Pearl Jones, a freelance stylist in the business of meticulously arranging food for the camera, points out that art and photography have often become more fanciful during periods of collective anxiety — not as denial, but as a sort of spiritual balm. “Through all the trauma that the world is experiencing,” she says, “there’s such a need for whimsy.” A tower offers permission to delight in something gloriously unnecessary.

That appeal mushrooms outward on social media. Because most food and drink towers are built from a single repeated ingredient — shrimp, Martinis, oysters, frilly tufts of radicchio — “you’re not really asking the viewer to do a lot of filtering or processing,” Jones says. The visual gag is instantly legible and delightful. And an image’s ability to halt scrolling thumbs has obvious benefits for restaurants.

The hot dog tower at Wally’s Wieners has become a siren song for tourists. “We have people travel from New Jersey and Connecticut and New York and Maine,” Head says. “They say, ‘We came to Newport just for Wally’s.’” Of course, he knows perfectly well that a hot dog is just a hot dog. But a lofty cairn of dogs? That becomes something else entirely: a moment that pulls us in, a photo worth sharing, and a memory that has a chance of holding on. “It’s fun,” Head says. “That’s all it is.”

title: Ask a Bartender: Can You Skip the Tip Line But Still Add Gratuity?
summary:
To tip or not to tip is never the question. (Always tip.) But after a three-Martini lunch or a wine tasting dinner, calculating the tip and the exact total can feel tedious or overwhelming. Instead, it might be tempting to just add the total amount on the bottom of the receipt, skipping the tip line altogether. So, is it feasible to add a gratuity without penning any amount on a receipt’s tip line at all?

The article Ask a Bartender: Can You Skip the Tip Line But Still Add Gratuity? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
To tip or not to tip is never the question. (Always tip.) But after a three-Martini lunch or a wine tasting dinner, calculating the tip and the exact total can feel tedious or overwhelming. Instead, it might be tempting to just add the total amount on the bottom of the receipt, skipping the tip line altogether.

So, is it feasible to add a gratuity without penning any amount on a receipt’s tip line at all? That’s a question that was spurred on by a recent Threads post, where a user claimed his “restaurant worker friends” said customers can just write “MATH” on the tip line and the total where indicated.

It seems like a pretty viable hack: Just write the grand total, tip included, to avoid doing the pesky math. With a topic as contentious as tipping, the post understandably gained some traction, with patrons and industry folk alike chiming in with their thoughts on the workaround. “The only thing that matters is the total line,” one user commented. Others noted that it’s not as straightforward.

To see how those behind the stick actually feel about guests skipping the tip line, VinePair tapped bartenders Ashtyn “Ash” Harris and Shammai Mading to find out. While it may be an easy fix for customers, it turns out what guests write or don’t write on a receipt is much trickier than it may seem.

Harris, pedigreed bartender at the well-reviewed Press Club in Washington, D.C., says the hack is technically sound. “If the guest just wants to put the total, they can do that and not stress about the math part for the tip,” she says. “It would make their lives easier.” But mental math is grounds for frequent error, so Harris prefers referencing both the tip and total line to make sure guests never feel swindled. Double-checking both requires the guest writing the tip and total on the physical check.

“Technically, the total is all that matters,” she says. “However, given the fact that customers are getting intoxicated, their math can be off, so I like to cross reference between tip and total.”

Handheld point-of-sale (POS) systems are one way to alleviate any mental math and confusion about what a grand total should be. In recent years, these mobile machines have become popular at many bars, prompting guests to select a tip percentage and doing the math for them.

“The bars I work at have handheld POS systems, so we don’t have to enter the tip amount because guests do that themselves by clicking a percentage amount,” says Mading, who splits her time between nouveau pub Banshee and Mexican-American cocktail bar Superbueno in Manhattan’s East Village.

That said, when Mading needs to print out a receipt, she likes when guests write the tip amount onto the check. “I need the added tip amount to enter into the POS,” she says. “The total doesn’t matter too much except to confirm that what someone wrote for the tip is correct.”

Mathematical errors may cause bartenders to compromise their own earnings to ensure a guest doesn’t feel scammed by a higher-than-expected total. For example, if a guest receives a bill for $50, and the guest adds a $10 tip but writes the total as $62, Harris will sacrifice those $2.

“We often close out checks at the end of the night when the guests are already gone,” she says. “I usually do what I imagine the guests intended, even if that means that I make a little less. I would hate for a guest to check their bank account the next day, lose their trust, and not come back. It’s a big integrity thing for me.”

Ultimately, it would be best for a guest to thoroughly write out both the tip and total line to avoid any confusion — and, ideally, with the correct math. The more information a guest can provide to the bartender handling the POS system, the better.

“I like full transparency,” Harris says. “The worst is when the guest feels like they can’t trust you or the establishment.”

News to know:

  • Family feud at Brown-Forman: Two members of the Brown family — which holds a controlling stake in the legendary whiskey company — addressed a scathing letter to the spirits producer’s board in early July, reports reveal. Heirs to the Brown-Forman fortune W. L. Lyons Brown III and Stuart Brown accused the board of “rewarding failure” and hemorrhaging “billions of dollars of generational wealth for the Brown family and all other shareholders,” according to the Wall Street Journal, who reviewed the internal memo. The two flamed the company’s board out for keeping them in the dark about recent merger talks with Pernod Ricard and Louisville neighbor Sazerac. In the past three years, Brown-Forman’s stock value has tumbled from the mid-$70s to the mid-$20s, the letter notes.
  • A walkout looms at Cameronbridge Distillery: Members of the Unite the Union organization at the Diageo-owned Scotland distillery — home to the production of a broad portfolio of brands like Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, and Tanqueray — opened a ballot to decide whether or not to strike. The walkout threat comes after Diageo’s chief executive officer Dave Lewis announced the company would shed thousands of jobs as part of his $1 billion cost-cutting plan.
  • Sazerac tacks a fourth distillery onto its Kentucky portfolio: The Louisville, Ky.-based spirits producer acquired Garrard County Distilling. It joins Barton 1792, The Glenmore, and Buffalo Trace as Sazerac’s lineup of its Bluegrass State-based distilleries.
  • Beer purchases during 2026 World Cup final outpace Super Bowl sales: A new report from consumer data and insights firm NielsenIQ reveals on-premise beer sales during the final match of the 2026 World Cup outperformed this year’s Super Bowl by 20 percent. The tournament’s final was beer’s most successful Sunday of the year for on-premise sales.

Product releases to watch:

  • Angel’s Envy adds a new finish to its Distillery Series: The premium American whiskey brand’s latest release in its limited-edition collection is a bourbon aged in ex-stout and ex-amburana barrels. The whiskey will be available at the Angel’s Envy Louisville distillery beginning Sept. 10 for a suggested retail price of $54.99.

title: The Honey Deuce Has a New Challenger at This Year’s US Open: Meet the Moët Serve
summary:
In the two decades since the Honey Deuce first debuted at the US Open, the drink has arguably become even more of a draw than the game itself. Tennis fans miss entire sets while standing in line for the cocktail, while others stack souvenir cups to show off how many combinations of Grey Goose vodka, lemonade, and raspberry liqueur they’ve consumed that afternoon. But this year, a fresh tennis-themed drink is vying to dethrone the tournament’s defending champion at the bar.

The article The Honey Deuce Has a New Challenger at This Year’s US Open: Meet the Moët Serve appeared first on VinePair.
content:
In the two decades since the Honey Deuce first debuted at the US Open, the drink has arguably become even more of a draw than the game itself. Tennis fans miss entire sets while standing in line for the cocktail, while others stack souvenir cups to show off how many combinations of Grey Goose vodka, lemonade, and raspberry liqueur they’ve consumed that afternoon.

But this year, a fresh tennis-themed drink is vying to dethrone the tournament’s defending champion at the bar. The US Open’s newest cocktail is called the Moët Serve and it’s a simple combination of bubbles provided by Moët & Chandon, the official Champagne of the event, a squeeze of lime, and ice.

The specs might not sound like much. But served in a collectible cup that looks like a tennis ball canister with three lime wheel garnishes stacked up to resemble tennis balls, it precisely follows the formula for iconic sporting event drinks like the Honey Deuce and Pimm’s Cup so it will surely appear on your Instagram feed a lot over the next few weeks.

The drink uses Moët Ice Impérial, a bottle that was released by the brand in 2010 as the first Champagne designed to be served with ice. Clocking in with a dosage of 45 grams/liter, the bubbles fall solidly into demi-sec territory, which is typically considered quite sweet — especially compared to the brand’s flagship bottle, Moët & Chandon Brut Impérial, which uses a dosage of 7 grams/liter. The increased sugar dials up the fruity notes already present in the wine and adds sweetness that could be considered cloying in most contexts. But in this case, when the bubbles cascade over cubes of ice, the intensity levels out.

While the cocktail is by no means complex, neither is its predecessor. The Honey Deuce is a simple vodka lemonade at its core, and with most iterations using big-brand bottled lemonades, it can also be quite sugary.

Instead of going for artisanal ingredients or ambitious technique, the Honey Deuce aimed to capture the zeitgeist with a garnish of three scoops of honeydew melon that look like tennis balls perched on top of the glass, and it clearly worked. Last year, the three-week tournament sold more than 738,000 Honey Deuces and raked in $17 million, a 32 percent year-over-year increase.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Lev Akabas, Data Visualization (@datakabas)

With three lime wheels pressed up against the side of the canister-shaped cup, the Moët Serve also leans on its photo-worthy garnish, which is no-doubt compelling to a certain set of tournament goers. Plus, like the Honey Deuce, Moët’s signature drink will also be available beyond the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center grounds at select locations throughout New York City, including Dante, Electric Lemon, and The St. Regis New York.

Though the Moët Serve might be a worthy competitor, the Honey Deuce still has a clear step up in maintaining its title as the most iconic drink of the event. First of all, there’s no denying home court advantage. The US Open is clear Honey Deuce territory, and it has widened its domain beyond the court as well, so much so that it feels like most bars across NYC offer their own take on the Honey Deuce during the tournament. It’s become so much of a status symbol, it’s hard for many fans to imagine going to a match without snapping a pic of their Honey Deuce as proof they were there.

The other obstacle the Moët Serve will no doubt encounter is its lofty price tag. At $23, the Honey Deuce was already considered a splurge for attendees, but the Moët Serve will be available for $32 — a steep increase, even by stadium standards. It’s unclear how many people are willing to shell out $9 more for a newcomer, even if it is Champagne-based.

So while the Honey Deuce is entering the tournament as the top seeded drink, the Moët Serve’s simplicity and eye-catching garnish could make it the dark horse to win the major this year. Though, it’d be a real upset.

title: Monster Beverage Is Making More Money Than Its Brewing Division Can Lose
summary:
Gambling is fun. Unless you lose. Unless-unless you were gambling with house money the whole time. In which case, who cares? Hold that thought. Earlier this month, Monster Beverage Corporation (MBC) reported its earnings for the second quarter of 2026. They were pretty spectacular. “Net sales, excluding the alcohol brand segment, increased 20.8 percent” in the three months through June 30, said chief executive Hilton Schlosberg on the company’s earnings call on August 6. The growth is remarkable given Monster’s age — it was founded in 2002 — and the challenges faced by upstart rivals like Celsius in this market.

The article Monster Beverage Is Making More Money Than Its Brewing Division Can Lose appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Gambling is fun. Unless you lose. Unless-unless you were gambling with house money the whole time. In which case, who cares?

Hold that thought. Earlier this month, Monster Beverage Corporation (MBC) reported its earnings for the second quarter of 2026. They were pretty spectacular.

“Net sales, excluding the alcohol brand segment, increased 20.8 percent” in the three months through June 30, said chief executive Hilton Schlosberg on the company’s earnings call on August 6. The growth is remarkable given Monster’s age — it was founded in 2002 — and the challenges faced by upstart rivals like Celsius in this market. (The latter brand’s revenue declined almost 12 percent on the quarter, though it was buoyed by strong performance from Alani Nu, which it acquired in 2025.) And of course, there’s the “Trump trade war” of it all to contend with, though Schlosberg told analysts he didn’t expect Monster to experience much harm from the tariffs beyond “a continued modest sequential increase in our aluminum costs through at least the end of 2026.” Yes, things are going very well indeed for Monster Beverage Corporation these days, and it has the $90-billion market capitalization to show for it.

Of course, this is a beer column, and as such, you will likely have noticed that Monster’s CEO conspicuously carved out Monster Brewing Company from these top-line results. “Excluding the alcohol brand segment from our reported results is purely illustrative as it remains part of our ongoing operations,” Schlosberg said. Which is a bit of an issue, because while MBC is raking in the chips, its bev-alc division is crapping out faster than Tim Robinson in a toupee.

Through the second quarter of the year, Monster Brewing posted a year-over-year net sales decrease of 15.2 percent, or $32.2 million. Not to put too fine a point on it, but that’s bad compared to both the overall beer business, and the craft brewing segment, neither of which are doing particularly well at the moment. It’s even bad compared to the division’s own first-quarter performance, when it managed to eke out a net sales loss of just 5.9 percent. The World Cup, which really hit its programming stride once the knockout round began just days before the end of Q2 on June 28, delivered very mixed results for the category, as Hop Take has previously reported. By the looks of off-premise scans, at least, the stretch since the quarter’s close has been a real mixed bag for Monster Brewing, too.

The CANarchy Craft Brewery Collective — the network of half a dozen craft-beer brands that MBC acquired in 2022 for $330 million to jumpstart its bev-alc ambitions — has actually performed decently well in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market-research firm Circana, posting mid-to-low single-digit percentages on dollar growth and just-barely there volume growth in two consecutive 30-day frames through mid-August. This is hardly gangbusters stuff, but it’s outpacing the category, which was slightly in the red on both measures for both periods. Cigar City’s Jai Alai, the closest thing Monster Brewing has to a company-wide beer flagship, is up 6.3 percent in dollars and 2.5 percent in volume year-to-date through August 9 — a darn solid result in this market, even if that growth has decelerated a bit in the most recent four weeks.

The portfolio formerly known as CANarchy is meaningfully larger than Monster Brewing’s “everything else” bucket, which is led by its Beast Unleashed flavored malt beverage. But the point of MBC’s nine-figure buy-in nearly five years ago was to set up the beverage juggernaut with a turnkey “platform” of production infrastructure, routes to market, and so forth that would allow it to quickly transmogrify its energy-drink marketing prowess into drink-drink revenues with new brands that could fill niches out of reach to traditional brewers.

This was sound logic, and it continues to be, what with virtually all the bev-alc growth opportunities coming from the flavor-forward meta-segment. The top 10 vendors in beer, wine, and spirits — 27 companies in total, because a few overlap — grew NIQ-tracked off-premise dollars of what Bump Williams Consulting calls “flavored alcohol” by 31.4 percent over the 52 weeks through June 6, compared to the same period in 2022. That figure, calculated by the longtime trade consultancy and first reported by Brewbound earlier this month, overshadows the moderating growth year-over-year between 2025 and 2026, when the cohort — larded with entries from new brands and cannibalizing extensions from existing firms — was up 3.3 percent. But that’s still better than those vendors’ “traditional” sales last year, which were down 3.3 percent in dollars.

The thing is, despite its tastebud-pwning pedigree, Monster Brewing has not figured out how to ride the flavor wave. After showing some early promise, The Beast Unleashed has struggled mightily to find a dedicated, scaled consumer base. Its rollout this year of Perfect 10, a 10-percent alcohol-by-volume tallboy primed to compete with the Twisted Tea Extremes and White Claw Surges of the gas-station fridge, came and went with nary a whisper. MBC understands the convenience-store channel’s thirsty customer about as well as any firm in the country, but its non-beer offerings have been getting clobbered. Monster Brewing LLC (under which Circana buckets all the company’s beyond-beer stuff) is down 21.9 percent in dollars and 23.7 in volume year-to-date in the latest scan sheet. What’s worse: those losses are accelerating in the most recent four-week period. The Beast Unleashed does not have a meaningful on-premise footprint. For the foreseeable future, the c-store is the ballgame, and Monster Brewing is losing it.

This raises two questions. The first is: what gives? How did MBC, with a sophisticated marketing operation mind-melded to the American manosphere’s drywall-punching id and visions of bev-alc grandeur, wind up with a mid-major craft-beer business that’s substantively outperforming its new flavored brands in a market that’s down on craft and up on flavor? You can chalk some of this up to the operational vagaries of the bev-alc business. Rodney Sacks, Schlosberg’s former co-CEO, told analysts as much in January 2025 by way of explaining an upcoming impairment charge MBC was then planning to take on the brewing division. (It was a doozy, bringing the company’s total bev-alc write-downs to $181.5 million in March 2025; that number soared in March 2026 to $232.4 million, or roughly 70 percent of the original purchase price.)

There’s also the gaping hole in Monster Brewing’s portfolio where a spirits-based ready-to-drink offering should be. As consumers have shifted to that format, major bev-alc firms from Anheuser-Busch InBev to the Mark Anthony Group have acquired brands to follow that spending. Even Molson Coors made an M&A move in that direction, acquiring Monaco Cocktails earlier this year. That’s the way the wind is blowing, especially in the c-store, where loosening rules around placements have allowed spirits-based stuff more market access. Monster Brewing is missing out on that entire market.

This brings us to the second question, which is in dialogue with the first: how much does this matter? For a company like, say, Tilray Brands, its bev-alc division matters a lot, especially since federal legalization of recreational marijuana use remains such a quagmire. The Canadian conglomerate’s dozens of craft breweries are “one of Tilray’s most important growth engines,” as CEO Irwin Simon put it on an earnings call last month. That’s just not true for MBC. With the overall company firing on all cylinders and racking up serious net-sales growth from its core business, its brewing division doesn’t have to stir its own drink. Whether this has engendered a lack of urgency within Monster Brewing is impossible to say from the outside looking in. (If you’d like to tell me about it, get in touch: dave@dinfontay.com. Anonymity available.) For now, it’s playing with house money in a sense.

Of course, MBC is a publicly traded company, not a casino. And at some point, the house money usually runs out. When the day comes for Monster Brewing to roll the dice for its own dinner, will it come up big, or go bust? If I had to place a bet today, I know which one I’d stack my chips behind. But for now, the game goes on.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

Last week, the Washington Examiner published an “exclusive” report on a poll that purported to show that 65 percent of likely voters would back tariffs on Mexican beer, with 89 percent “support[ing] policies that protect American beer jobs and businesses.” This is good fodder for the Teamsters, who have been angling to get the Trump administration to make Modelo’s supply-chain costs expensive enough for parent company Constellation Brands that it decides to bring those brewing jobs north of the border. Whatever merit that scheme has, though, this data has less: it was produced by John McLaughlin, a pollster so MAGA-brained that the national Republican Party at one point warned its candidates against relying on his work.

📈 Ups…

Speaking of Constellation’s intra-continental route to market, its beer division just hired a new chief supply chain officer… Allagash Brewing Co. has a new national sales director… Tune in to your humble Hop Take columnist on recent episodes of The Brewbound Podcast and North Catch… Ninkasi Brewing acquired some $400,000 worth of Rogue Ales & Spirits barrel inventory at auction…

📉 …and downs

Sapporo USA plans to lay off 220 workers as it closes down former Stone Brewing locations in Southern California… The Brewers Association is bidding farewell to its state government affairs director…

title: From Santorini to the Canary Islands: 7 Volcanic Wine Regions Beyond Mt. Etna Worth Exploring
summary:
Mount Etna’s recent eruption reminded the world just how powerful volcanoes can be. For wine lovers, lava flow isn’t something to fear; rather, it’s celebrated as the source of compelling terroir. And while Etna, even when not exploding, often steals the spotlight, other regions around the world boast these unique soils. “Volcanic wines” is an umbrella term for wines made from highly complex and varied soils originating from those fiery, smoking craters. During explosions, different volcanoes emit different types of lava, with varying levels of silicon dioxide.

The article From Santorini to the Canary Islands: 7 Volcanic Wine Regions Beyond Mt. Etna Worth Exploring appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Mount Etna’s recent eruption reminded the world just how powerful volcanoes can be. For wine lovers, lava flow isn’t something to fear; rather, it’s celebrated as the source of compelling terroir. And while Etna, even when not exploding, often steals the spotlight, other regions around the world boast these unique soils.

“Volcanic wines” is an umbrella term for wines made from highly complex and varied soils originating from those fiery, smoking craters. During explosions, different volcanoes emit different types of lava, with varying levels of silicon dioxide. Along the way, the outflow picks up and moves other matter down hillsides and into valleys, creating unique layers of soil, all of which contribute to standout wines. It’s challenging terroir to farm, given the often hot, rugged terrain. In the case of Etna, you have to be somewhat of an adrenaline junkie to want to work in proximity to an active volcano, day in and day out.

But on the plus side, volcanic soils are inhospitable to pests and disease, which makes organic farming easier than in many other regions. The soils have also preserved old indigenous grape varieties. Trademark styles of volcanic wines include high acidity, salinity, and nuanced savory — rather than fruit — flavors in the forefront.

Some wine regions that benefit from volcanic soils are no longer home to active volcanoes, but still boast the complex, layered soils from eruptions of the past. Here are seven other volcanic regions beyond Mount Etna to know for wine.

Soave, Italy

Sixty-five million years ago, Soave was underwater. But subterranean explosions in fissures where the African plate had collided with the Eurasian plate created volcanoes. Over millions of years, the explosions started filling in the lagoon where Soave now stands. Volcanoes haven’t been active for 25 million years, but you can still taste the imprint on the wines. Garganega is the main grape here, although Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay sometimes make their way into blends. Like Chardonnay, Garganega is a fairly neutral grape that does a great job of expressing terroir. Orchard fruit, high acidity, and a through-line of acidity shine in the best wines. Producers to try: Suavia, Inama, and Pieropan.

Santorini, Greece

The island is due for a big eruption in the next 20 years, said Yiannis Paraskevopoulos of Gaia Wines in 2023. Located in what’s called the Hellenic Volcanic Arc, Santorini sits in one of the most volcanically active areas in the world. That hasn’t stopped the tourists from coming, however — or winemakers from tending to their centuries-old vines. Because of the dry and windy climate, vines are often trained in a basket shape, low to the ground. This protects vines from flying debris and breakage. The lack of disease pressure makes it possible to find vines over 200 years old. When it comes to wine, the island is best known for the zippy, mineral-driven white variety Assyrtiko. While it’s grown elsewhere in Greece, no other region matches the depth of flavor, concentration, and acidity of Santorini. Producers to try: Gaia Wines, Domaine Sigalas, and Estate Argyros.

Canary Islands, Spain

Volcanoes played a major role in developing the Canary Islands’ wine industry. On the one hand, volcanic explosions, such as a major one in Tenerife in 1706, closed ports and stunted trade. But at the same time, being closed off from international influence allowed native grapes to flourish. And given that phylloxera never made an entrance, old-vine varieties like Listán Blanco and Listán Negro found a new generation of fans when intrepid winemakers started revitalizing the industry in the 1980s and 1990s. Lanzarote, another island in the archipelago, is also defined by its rocky, black volcanic terrain. Viticulture here can be pretty challenging: The intense heat and winds make the typical vine training patterns impossible, so producers here hand-dig individual holes in the ground called “hoyos” for each of the vines, protecting each one with a small rock wall around the edges. The Producers to try: Bodegas Los Bermejos, Bodega Matías i Torres, and Bodegas Viñátigo.

Tokaj, Hungary

Active volcanoes millions of years ago left their mark on the Hungarian landscape. While the tension and minerality from the soils can be felt throughout the country’s dry reds and whites, it adds a new dimension to one of the world’s most famous sweet wines: Tokaji Aszú. Botrytis develops from the nighttime fog that blankets vineyards, transforming Furmint, Hárslevelú, and Yellow Muscat grapes into shriveled, sweetened orbs. As John Szabo notes in his book, “Volcanic Wines,” some producers believe the soils, with their mineral content, protect the vines from nefarious rot, much as salt preserves food. Taste-wise, the savory, saline qualities give these sweet wines an edginess that elevates them above other sweet wines. Producers to try: Royal Tokaji and Oremus.

Willamette Valley, Ore.

Much of the Willamette Valley soil conversation centers around marine sedimentary soils, particularly in AVAs such as Yamhill-Carlton and Ribbon Ridge, but it’s only half the story. Volcanic Jory soil — known for its red color and well-draining properties — dominate in the Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, and Chehalem Mountains AVAs. (Jory soil was actually named the state soil of Oregon in 2011.) In general, volcanic soils give more red fruit qualities to Willamette’s iconic Pinot Noirs, while marine sediment offers a darker fruit expression. Producers to try: Evening Land, Bergström Wines, 00 Wines, and CHO Wines.

Auvergne, France

For a long time, the famous beverage in Auvergne was water — Vichy water from the namesake town’s natural springs, to be specific. But in recent years, a coterie of natural winemakers sprung up in this volcanic region in central France. As mentioned before, volcanic soils favorably aid organic viticulture and, by extension, low-intervention winemaking. The grape garnering the most attention is Gamay d’Auvergne, which yields darker and spicier wines than other Gamays in France. Producers to try: Marie and Vincent Tricot, Verdier-Logel, and Henri Chauvet.

Lake County, Calif.

The Lake County AVA, located north of Napa and Sonoma, boasts some of the highest elevation vineyards in California, with the dormant Mt. Konocti volcano and other mountains defining the terrain. The volcanic soils, along with large diurnal shifts and high UV exposure, produce red wines with grippy tannins, ample acidity, and a ton of body. Cabernet Sauvignon is the signature red variety, but a whole cornucopia of other varieties, including Zinfandel, Mourvèdre, Grenache, and Petite Sirah thrive in the altitudinous vineyards. Producers to try: Obsidian Ridge Wine Co., Brassfield Estate, and Six Sigma.
